heading: Vegetables and staple crops
body: Welcome. This is the lesson called Vegetables and staple crops. It is one of the ten training modules of ImbewuField.
A productive garden is not the one that looks full on one day. It is the one that keeps bringing food into the home, every week.
In the next few minutes we will talk about four things. How to build a bed. How to keep the harvests coming. Which staple crops you must grow. And what you must do when the pests arrive.

heading: Why it matters
body: Let us start with the problem.
One big sowing at once gives you an overflowing harvest. Everything is ready at the same time. You eat what you can, give some to others, and what is left over rots.
Then comes a gap. Nothing is ready. The garden is full of plants, but there is no food in it.
Sowing a little at a time creates a rhythm instead. Planting, tending and harvesting overlap. There is always something that is about to be ready.
That rhythm is what feeds the home. It is not the growth of the garden.

heading: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this module, you will be able to make four decisions on your field.
First. Build a suitable bed — match the width and type of the bed to your soil and your rain.
Second. Keep the harvests coming, using planting one after another and mixing crops.
Third. Choose staple crops that protect you when one crop does not succeed.
Fourth. Learn the problem of the pest before you treat it.
These four go together. A well-built bed may still fail if everything is planted on one day. Different planting may also fight against you if you think every yellow leaf is a problem of an insect.

heading: Roots need loose soil, paths need your feet
body: Compressed soil loses its air spaces. Roots slow down. Water goes in a different way. The bed becomes harder to work every season of the year.
Protecting is easy. Permanent paths, and a bed narrow enough that you can reach the middle from both sides.
A width of 1 to 1.2 metres. That is the working number. At such a width you can reach the middle from one of the paths, and your feet do not touch the growing area.
Now think about your beds. Can you reach the middle without stepping inside? Go and try that before you plant anything else.

heading: Choose a bed according to soil and rain
body: There is no one bed shape that is right everywhere.
Start with the way that disturbs the soil least, but that makes your problem simpler.
The no-digging way (no-dig) suits most garden soils. Do not disturb its structure, build up the richness of the soil on top.
Do not dig wet clay. If soil compaction or poor drainage of water is very bad, identify the cause by getting local advice before choosing to dig deeper.
Raised beds are suitable for wet soil, where the water needs a place it can go.
Sunken beds are suitable for dry soil, where you want to catch and keep the rain you get.
Look after heavy rain. Where does the water stay or where does it run off? Combine what you saw with advice on soil and on water draining away before choosing a bed.

heading: Seed or seedling?
body: Some crops do not like their roots being disturbed. They grow well when sown directly where they will grow. Beans, carrots and maize are in this group.
Others grow well when they start off protected in a place for sowing seed (nursery), then are moved to another place. Tomatoes and brassicas (plants of the cabbage family) are in this group.
Use the guide for the distance between plants according to the crop, its type and local conditions. Look at the seed packet and the advice of local farmers. Watch out for crowding as the plants grow.

heading: Mark out the working shape
body: Before you plant, mark the bed.
A width of 1.2 metres. A length of three metres. One bed for practising.
Use pegs and string. Mark a rectangle, and mark both access paths too.
Then prepare your soil — start with no digging, and dig deep only if your soil really needs it.
The string line turns an idea into a decision. When the paths are already there, keep them. When the growing area is already there, protect it.
That bed becomes easier to improve every season of the year, because you have stopped walking on it.

heading: A sowing rhythm keeps food moving
body: Planting one after another (succession planting) is a calendar habit, not a special crop.
Choose something your household eats often. Then sow a small amount of it, repeatedly.
Plant a short row every two to three weeks.
There is little spoilage when there is no overflowing harvest. Fresh food for a long time. And the work is spread through the season instead of falling on you all at once.
Sowing at different times can reduce the risk of losing everything at once. It does not guarantee a harvest if hard conditions continue.
Which fast crop can you sow in small groups? Choose one, and start this week.

heading: Sow a little, often
body: Here is how it looks in practice.
Sow one. Then after two to three weeks, sow two. Then sow three. Then sow four.
At the right time for the crop, the harvests can begin to meet. The first group is not always ready by the time of the fourth sowing.
Two to three weeks is a starting rhythm, not a law. A cool-season leafy crop can stay for a long time. Heat can hurry things up, or cause the crop to fail.
Watch what your garden does, and change the time between sowings. That watching is the real skill.

heading: Each crop gets its place
body: Mixing crops (intercropping) is not just crowding different crops together. Each crop needs a job, and enough space to do it.
The Three Sisters is an example from the farming traditions of the indigenous people of America (the Americas).
Maize gives height and structure.
Beans climb on the maize, and keep protein.
Pumpkin spreads on the ground, shading the soil and keeping it moist.
Timing matters. Start the maize first, so that it is strong enough to carry the beans when they begin to climb.

The crops may compete. Give them the right space, water and light. Beans capture nitrogen with the root bacteria, but do not take it that they feed the maize straight away; the nutrients in the leftovers are released during rotting.

heading: Plan backwards from your hungry gap
body: A household can have a hungry gap: weeks when the stored food runs low before the next harvest is ready.
Yours may come after the stored maize is finished. It may come before the green winter vegetables are ready. It may come in the dry season when water limits the garden.
Do not copy another person's calendar. Start by calling out the names of your months.
Write them down. Then choose a crop and a sowing date that puts food into that gap.
That is planning backwards, and it is what separates a garden that looks productive from a household that really eats.

heading: Staple crops protect you from going without food
body: A staple crop deserves its position because it feeds the household beyond the day of harvest.
It carries energy or protein. It is stored, or it stays in the soil until you need it. And often it also carries cultural memory.
One staple crop leaves you unprotected. Two or more give you a choice when weather or pests strike.
Grow at least two. Not one.
Which staple crop does your household depend on most right now? That is the one that would hurt most if it did not succeed — so that is the one that needs a partner.

heading: Different staple crops protect you from different dangers
body: Each staple crop protects you from something different.

Maize gives calories, and is kept dry. Open-pollinated maize (whose pollen is carried naturally by wind or insects) allows you to keep your own seed too, if you control the separation of crops (isolation) and selection.
Beans and cowpeas give a protein harvest that can be stored.

Sweet potato develops some drought tolerance after the storage roots have formed. It needs water in the first weeks even while the roots are forming; water stress at that time can reduce the harvest. Its young leaves are also eaten.
Amadumbe survive in wetter soil, where other staple crops struggle.
Note that they fail under different conditions. That is exactly the point.

heading: Variety keeps food moving
body: Tolerance does not mean that nothing fails.
It means that one failure does not end your household's food plan.
One crop is one place of failure.
Two or more staple crops give you many ways of continuing to eat.
Different crops use water, soil and times differently. That difference is protection.

heading: Pests are messengers before they are enemies
body: Pest stress rises for a reason.
Plants under stress. One crop that dominates the soil. Or the excessive use of chemicals has already removed the predators that were helping you.
So before you treat anything, look at the whole system.
Is the plant short of water? Is the soil compressed, or does it lack enough nutrients? Are the predators already working to make the problem simpler?
A yellow leaf is not automatically an insect. It can be water, feeding, or root damage. Know which it is before you do anything.

heading: Treat the cause before the insect
body: Follow four steps, in order.
First. Look. Look at how the damage looks, the underside of the leaf, the stem, and the plants nearby.
Second. Check for stress. Soil wetness, roots, distance between plants, feeding, water draining away.
Third. Protect those who help you. Helpful insects do work that you would otherwise do.

Fourth. Only after that, do something — and start with a simple thing that works. Removing physically, barriers or a change in the care of the crop can help. Make sure the action matches the problem and look at the results.

If treatment is needed, use a product registered for that crop and that pest, and follow its label. This includes neem products. Check the safety instructions and the waiting time before harvesting. Do not invent mixtures or stronger doses.
Be honest with yourself about which step you always skip.

heading: Field work
body: Now the lesson ends on the ground.
Build one bed that can keep on feeding. 1.2 metres by three metres.
Reach the middle from both sides. Keep every foot on the paths. Set the distance between plants according to your climate. Cover the bed with mulch.
Check the bed regularly from the planting. Use the ten-day photo as a place to check the work, not as a reason to delay care.
Take its photo once it has been planted. Then come back after ten days with what you saw.
The aim is not a perfect photo. The aim is a bed whose shape, plant spacing and rhythm you chose on purpose.

heading: Field action
body: This week, set one bed into production.
First. Mark the bed and the paths.
Second. Plant, with your spacing and your sowing rhythm.
Third. Come back after ten days, with a photo.
Then look. Adjust. And write down.
Write down the sowing date. The rain. What has sprouted. Pest stress. What you have harvested.
Over time, your garden depends a little on guessing, and depends more on what you have seen happening on your land.
Use your record together with trusted local advice when making the next decision.
